manuscript.positioning: bounded controlled persistent-web-agent first-violation case study

supported_claims: Within the frozen R9 BrowserART/HarmBench operationalization, a 12/12 current non-violation panel did not guarantee absence of first violations over the evaluated three-step future.

Within 12 frozen paired trajectories, updated workflows produced 8/12 event branches versus 4/12 under the same held-out schedule with the base workflow held fixed; paired discordance was 4 update-only to 0 control-only.
Four of 12 originally clean state-by-probe trajectories developed a first evaluator-classified violation at a later workflow snapshot while probe identity and seed were fixed.
not_supported_claims: The paired branch difference is a population causal effect.
Static safety evaluation is generally ineffective across agents, models, or benchmarks.
The observed branch event fractions are population hazards.
State identity is a statistically established predictor.
HarmBench labels are a noiseless safety oracle.
This work originates longitudinal memory-safety evaluation.

closest_source_collision.source: Al-Tawaha et al., Remembering More, Risking More, arXiv:2605.17830
closest_source_collision.effect: Their study has broader multi-architecture longitudinal coverage. R9 adopts same-schedule/base-memory and fixed-probe control logic but contributes an action-taking BrowserART/AWM trajectory comparison with branch first-event timing.

remaining_scope_limits: One backbone and four selected states do not support a population claim.
HarmBench has not been independently validated for this frozen BrowserART realization.
Fresh stochastic rollouts under matched seeds are controlled realized comparisons, not deterministic potential outcomes.
General longitudinal-memory-safety novelty is occupied by broader current work.
reopen_condition: separate persistent update effect from held-out schedule effect
reopen_control: same held-out schedule with the workflow held at its step-0 base state
